title: Integrate compact tiny-hypergraph candidate state
description: Integrates a compact candidate state for the tiny-hypergraph, reducing memory usage and improving solver performance.
body:
## Summary

- pin `tiny-hypergraph` to squash-merge commit [`c60c552`](https://github.com/tscircuit/tiny-hypergraph/commit/c60c55266323974507ca3de06ff6ff3c4860436d) from [tiny-hypergraph #164](https://github.com/tscircuit/tiny-hypergraph/pull/164)
- integrate compact legal-hop candidate storage, generation-scoped typed frontier state, and early dominated-candidate pruning
- leave the separate `tiny-hypergraph-poly` dependency unchanged

## Why

The upstream change replaces impossible `portCount * regionCount` candidate state with `portCount * maxPortIncidence` state. On the DDR5 regression fixture this reduces the two best-cost arrays from 4.21 GB to 662 KB and allows the solver to be constructed instead of risking an allocation crash.

Upstream's paired same-machine SRJ18 benchmark measured:

- 2.98x faster average `solveGraph`
- 2.72x faster total runtime
- 4.04x faster P95
- unchanged 100% completion
- average region cost 1.713 -> 1.739 (+1.5%)
- sample008 iterations 2,000,004 -> 1,197,441

See the [Same Machine Benchmark Results](https://github.com/tscircuit/tiny-hypergraph/pull/164#issuecomment-5263044765).

## Validation

- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bun run build`
- 10 focused tiny-hypergraph/Pipeline 7/Pipeline 9/partial-rip/reachability tests pass
- `/benchmark-all --same-machine` compared main `84be067` with integration commit `085623f`; the squash-merge commit has the identical Git tree as the benchmarked pre-merge commit

## Same-machine autorouter results

| Dataset | Completion | Relaxed DRC | Timing signal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [dataset01](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263192421) | 100% -> 100% | 98.8% -> 98.8% | P50 -7.2%, P95 -8.3% |
| [SRJ18](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263192621) | 56.3% -> 56.3% | 31.3% -> 31.3% | P50 -4.1%; P60-P95 timeout-capped |
| [SRJ19](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263192778) | 84.5% -> 84.0% | 40.0% -> 40.0% | P50 -0.4%, P80 -1.5%; one extra timeout |
| [SRJ20](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263192912) | 71.5% -> 71.5% | 37.5% -> 38.5% | P50 +1.2%, P60 +15.2%; mixed outcomes |
| [SRJ21](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263193008) | 100% -> 100% | 90.0% -> 90.0% | P50 -6.2%, P90 -8.0% |
| [SRJ23](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2083#issuecomment-5263193223) | 98.7% -> 98.7% | 14.5% -> 14.5% | P50 -10.4%, P95 -5.4% |

The integration is a repeatable 4-10% end-to-end speedup on the lighter/solved datasets, but not a universal large win. SRJ19 is effectively neutral with one completion regression, while SRJ20 is outcome-noisy and slower around P60. The upstream `solveGraph` speedup is diluted where detailed routing and 360-second timeouts dominate total runtime.

Build, type-check, format, Vercel build/deployment, and all eight CI test shards pass. Deterministic SVG route snapshots for bugreports 51, 58, 60, and 84 were updated from the failing Linux CI artifacts, with matching macOS expectations for 51 and 58. The four focused local bugreport tests also pass serially (5 pass, 0 fail).

title: Preserve copper clearance after broad repulsion
description: Fixes via-to-trace clearance violations caused by broad repulsion processing in autorouting, ensuring compliance with DRC requirements.
body:
## Summary

- run a single via-to-trace cleanup after obstacle pushes finish
- skip final cleanup for speculative periodic broad candidates that are immediately DRC-evaluated
- add the minimized SPI display interceptor repro with 3 routes and 2 obstacles
- add a focused before/after SVG snapshot of the failing clearance

## Root cause

Broad repulsion processed copper pairs before pad obstacles on every pass. A final pad push could therefore move a via back toward a different-net trace, and the pass could terminate with the newly introduced via-to-trace violation. In the captured case, clearance fell from 0.176 mm to 0.083 mm even though 0.1 mm was required.

The final targeted cleanup resolves residual via-to-trace interactions without another obstacle pass overwriting them. It runs once, so unrelated copper pair geometry and broad-repulsion runtime remain stable. The minimized regression finishes with zero DRC errors.

Profiling found that cleanup itself only cost about 4 ms per call, but applying it to every speculative periodic candidate changed branch selection on SRJ18 `sample004` and caused four additional broad passes. Direct and final broad outputs retain cleanup; speculative candidates skip it because the caller immediately performs an exact DRC evaluation. This removes the observed hotspot without weakening the reproduced fix.

The visual regression snapshot zooms into the affected via and foreign trace, comparing the captured 0.083 mm failure with the repaired 0.111 mm result. The red/green clearance radius represents the minimum allowed different-net trace centerline distance.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 60 passed, 0 failed
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run formatcheck`
- focused repro — 0.176 mm input clearance, 0.111 mm output clearance, zero DRC errors
- same-runner ABBA SRJ18, concurrency 4 — 69.86 s PR vs 70.47 s base (-0.85%), identical final DRC
- same-runner ABBA SRJ18, concurrency 1 — 40.18 s PR vs 40.62 s base (-1.09%), identical final DRC

title: [BENCHMARK TEST] Run paired benchmarks on one runner
description: Run benchmarks for the PR head and its exact base SHA in the same GitHub Actions job to control for machine-to-machine variance and ensure consistent benchmarking results.
body:
## Summary

- benchmark the PR head and its exact base SHA in ABBA order in the same GitHub Actions job
- install each checkout independently and forward identical benchmark arguments to both
- compare the paired reports in the job summary and `/benchmark` comment
- resolve workflow-dispatch branch names and short SHAs to immutable full commits before checkout
- keep the existing main-branch benchmark artifacts for historical results

## Why

The current `/benchmark` comparison downloads the latest successful main-branch artifact. That baseline may have run hours earlier on a different hosted runner, so machine-to-machine variance is reported as a code delta. It also only checks that the dataset matches; custom concurrency, effort, scenario limit, and iteration arguments can differ.

This workflow checks out the PR head and the PR's exact base SHA into separate directories, then runs both with the same arguments on one runner. Each revision runs twice in base/PR/PR/base order, and the per-sample times are averaged. This controls both runner-to-runner variance and cold-cache, warm-up, or thermal ordering bias.

## Validation

- workflow YAML parses successfully
- `bun run formatcheck`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun test` — 59 passed, 0 failed
- self-comparison with identical solver code — PR 89.11 s vs base 89.97 s (-0.95%), demonstrating approximately 1% residual measurement noise

The `[BENCHMARK TEST]` title intentionally exercises the paired workflow on this PR.

title: Remove Sharp from SVG snapshots
description: Removes the Sharp dependency from SVG snapshot testing by upgrading to bun-match-svg0.0.16 and using an alternative comparison method, preserving existing SVG snapshot behavior without requiring Sharp.
body:
## What changed

- Upgrade `bun-match-svg` from `0.0.15` to `0.0.16`.
- Use the matcher's `@tscircuit/image-utils/looks-same` implementation instead of the legacy Sharp-backed comparator.
- Remove the direct `sharp` development dependency and trusted dependency entry.
- Remove the manual Sharp installation script and run tests with plain `bun test`.

## Why

The previous matcher depended on `looks-same@9`, which pinned `sharp@0.32.6`. This caused unrelated GitHub Actions jobs to fail during `bun install` when Sharp's native binary installation failed. `bun-match-svg@0.0.16` delegates comparison to `@tscircuit/image-utils/looks-same` and does not require Sharp as a consumer dependency.

## Impact

Fresh installs no longer need Sharp or its native installation step. Existing SVG snapshot behavior is preserved.

## Validation

- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run test` — 32 passed, including every SVG snapshot
- Focused SVG snapshot tests — 9 passed

title: Speed up dense board routing
description: Optimizes the A search algorithm in the autorouter by caching heuristics and reducing overhead, resulting in significant performance improvements without altering routing decisions.
body:
## What changed

- Cache target heuristics, demand allowances, ownership lookups, and penalty tables for each active A* search.
- Store packed state keys and blocker states once instead of rebuilding and re-hashing them when states are popped.
- Remove per-entry heap object allocation by keeping values and priorities in parallel arrays.
- Reuse clearance checkers while beautifying each trace.
- Add exact bounding-box rejection before expensive obstacle/net and segment-distance checks.

## Why

The RP2040 benchmark was dominated by repeated invariant work in the A* inner loop and by exhaustive geometric clearance scans during post-processing and beautification. These changes reduce that overhead without changing route order, routing decisions, or board-specific behavior.

## Impact

The four-board benchmark still routes every demand with the universal `adaptive` default. RP2040 improved from roughly 95.8s before this optimization to 70.4s in the full validation run (and 66.2s in an isolated run), while preserving the same 97/97 result, 26,510,022 expanded states, zero manufactured vias, and zero clearance violations. Post-processing fell from about 4.5–5.1s to 1.1s, and beautification from about 29.5–34.8s to 6.6s.

## Validation

- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`
- `bun test` — 32 passed
- `./benchmark.sh` — 4/4 boards passed under the 180s per-board timeout
  - STM32: 0.8s
  - STM32 display: 5.5s
  - STM32 display BoosterPack: 6.6s
  - RP2040: 70.4s

title: Use adaptive routing for biscuit boards
description: Make adaptive the single default route policy for every board, prioritizing pending demands from topology, endpoint availability, current occupancy, and congestion history, while preserving negotiated conflict-component queue order for reroutes.
body:
## Summary

- make `adaptive` the single default route policy for every board
- prioritize pending demands from topology, endpoint availability, current occupancy, and congestion history
- preserve negotiated conflict-component queue order for reroutes to avoid repeating local cycles
- replace RP2040-specific connection-name and route-ID checks with structural rules for fine-pitch corridors, dense junction escapes, and sparse-net crossing protection
- retain explicit static `routeOrder` values only as backwards-compatible overrides
- use Euclidean segment-to-obstacle distance for final clearance validation, including rotated rectangles and circles
- add benchmark stage timing, peak committed-demand telemetry, adaptive-priority coverage, and updated routing regressions

## Root cause

The previous optimization conditionally selected a static longest-first order for a dense board by checking the demand count and `source_trace_*` names. The router also contained route-name special cases for several RP2040 corridors. Those rules encoded fixture identity instead of adapting to the actual routing problem.

The replacement derives its decisions from terminal count, net topology, endpoint degree, pad geometry, graph blockage, current ownership, and accumulated congestion. Routing decisions no longer inspect connection-name prefixes or specific route IDs.

## Impact

All four benchmark boards pass in one run with the same default policy:

- STM32: 0.9s
- STM32 display: 5.8s
- STM32 display BoosterPack: 7.1s
- RP2040: 95.8s

Every case emits its full demand count with no manufactured vias and no clearance violations. RP2040 completes 97/97 demands within the 180-second limit.

The adaptive scheduler also has a focused synthetic regression where live endpoint constraints override its topology prior.

## Validation

- `./benchmark.sh --progress-ms=30000` — 4/4 passed
- `bun run test` — 32 passed
- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`
- `git diff --check`

body:
## Summary

- replace the RP2040-only benchmark with a suite covering the STM32C071, STM32 display, STM32 display BoosterPack, and RP2040 boards
- capture the complete BoosterPack Simple Route JSON fixture
- omit `routeOrder` from every case so the solver's default is exercised
- preserve each board's other problem-specific tuning
- continue through failures/timeouts and emit a single aggregate JSON report
- default each case to a 180-second timeout

Repros 03 and 04 have byte-identical routing inputs, so the suite runs that problem once rather than double-counting two visual crops.

## Why

This creates a stable baseline for choosing route order automatically or changing the routing paradigm. It also makes the failure mode measurable across representative real boards instead of optimizing solely for RP2040.

## Current baseline

With the solver default `input` order:

- STM32C071 passes in about 1.1 seconds
- STM32 display routes 33/33 demands in about 5.5 seconds but reports 11 clearance violations
- STM32 display BoosterPack passes in about 11.5 seconds
- RP2040 does not finish within 180 seconds

The 180-second RP2040 sample reached 93/97 routes at 120–150 seconds. At cutoff it had 92/97 routes, 3 conflict routes, 665 negotiation passes, 5,329 rips, and 78.9M expanded states. The routed count is non-monotonic because rip-and-replace temporarily disconnects routes during negotiation.

## Validation

- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`

- `./benchmark.sh --case=stm32 --max-ms=10000 --json`
- `./benchmark.sh --case=rp2040 --progress-ms=30000` — expected nonzero baseline after the 180-second timeout

title: Fix irregular trace expansion near pads
description: Fixes irregular trace expansion near pads by ensuring nominal trace width is carried into route demands and adding escape corridors for better routing around obstacles.
body:
## Summary

- carry nominal trace width into route demands and prefer paths with enough static-obstacle clearance for the final width
- add guarded nominal-width terminal escape corridors while preserving physical-width escape nodes as fallbacks
- refresh the expected SVGs for the existing `R_USER_LED` and button-board snapshot tests

## Root cause

The primary router originally considered only the 0.25 mm physical width. This placed traces exactly at the physical-width pad-clearance boundary before the later expansion to 0.30 mm.

The first fix let ordinary routes prefer nominal-width clearance, which corrected `R_USER_LED`. The remaining power-LED route used a mandatory terminal escape ending at the physical-width boundary. The expander then repaired individual subintervals around `R_PWR_LED` and `D_PWR`, producing shallow-angle jogs and mixed widths.

The graph now offers both the original physical escape and a guarded nominal-width escape. Routing prefers the expansion-safe corridor, but the physical corridor remains available when congestion makes it necessary.

## Summary

Increase the per-board autorouter timeout used by the board asset generator from 600 seconds to 900 seconds.

## Why

The `Build BoosterPack Site` workflow failed on push to `main` because the existing `boostxl-drv8305evm` board exceeded the 600-second routing limit. The other 12 boards, including the newly added boards, completed successfully.

## Impact

Slow, performance-sensitive board routes receive 50% more time to complete while remaining within the workflow's 30-minute job timeout.

## Validation

- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun test` (5 passed)
- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run build:site` (13 static board routes created)

A full asset regeneration was not rerun locally because the failing board can take more than 10 minutes; the change only updates the existing `tsci --autorouter-timeout` argument.

title: Use dedicated Circuit JSON to Altium package
description: Generates Altium downloads through the dedicated circuit-json-to-altium package, removing the previous converter implementation and retaining a single integration test for the package boundary.
body:
## Summary

- generate Altium downloads through the dedicated [`circuit-json-to-altium`](https://github.com/tscircuit/circuit-json-to-altium/pull/1) package
- pin its reviewed feature commit exactly at `b7027586888496a21c8531fffd2f871068d5f64d`
- remove the 2,124 lines of converter implementation and detailed exporter tests that no longer belong in the BoosterPacks application
- retain one consumer integration test for the package boundary

## Dependency chain

- `boosterpacks.tscircuit.com` pins `circuit-json-to-altium` PR #1 by immutable commit
- `circuit-json-to-altium` pins [`altiumts` PR #43](https://github.com/tscircuit/altiumts/pull/43) at immutable commit `043a6e90be8106ad3e0319ba2797d0a0a464f73a`
- `altiumts` owns native Altium parsing, models, sanitization, and binary serialization
- `circuit-json-to-altium` owns Circuit JSON mapping, geometry/connectivity policy, and project archive assembly
- BoosterPacks now owns only invocation and delivery of the generated archive

## Converter coverage

The dedicated package has 11 test cases in 11 test files covering archive structure, filename and field sanitization, board geometry, transitive net merging, pads and holes, routed copper and vias, silkscreen, schematic primitives, multiple sheets, and deterministic randomized inputs.

Its validation includes 14 real fixtures from `circuit-json-to-kicad`: 10,716 Circuit JSON elements, 6,892 PCB records, and 2,631 schematic records. Every generated document passed strict validation, with zero dangling PCB references and zero schematic ownership cycles.

## BoosterPacks validation

- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run lint`
- `bun run typecheck`

title: Write native binary Altium exports for Altium 365 Viewer
description: Changes the export format for Altium files to native binary, allowing direct compatibility with Altium 365 Viewer and ensuring correct board contour orientation.
body:
## What changed

- write `.PcbDoc` and `.SchDoc` as native OLE/CFB Altium binary documents instead of legacy ASCII files with modern extensions
- serialize board geometry, nets, components, pads, tracks, and vias into their native Altium PCB streams
- normalize board contours to Altium's clockwise winding, including explicit Circuit JSON outlines and rectangular width/height fallbacks
- serialize schematic sheets and records into native Altium block streams
- keep the editable `.PrjPcb` project archive and validate every generated document before packaging
- add regression coverage for CFB signatures, PCB primitives, schematic contents, exact board bounds, clockwise outline winding, and the absence of Gerber/drill fallbacks

## Root cause

The exporter generated valid legacy ASCII Protel/Altium records, but named them `.PcbDoc` and `.SchDoc`. Altium 365 Viewer did not recognize that legacy container variant and rejected the whole archive before parsing the records.

The export now preserves the existing Circuit JSON conversion while encoding those records in the native compound-file structures that current Altium tooling expects.

A follow-up comparison with TI's original native BOOSTXL-AUDIO `.PcbDoc` also found that generated contours wound counterclockwise. Altium board-region contours are clockwise, so the exporter now normalizes their winding before serialization.

## User impact

The Altium download from BoosterPack board pages, including BOOSTXL-AUDIO, opens directly in Altium 365 Viewer as a CAD project with a correctly oriented board contour. The archive contains no Gerber or drill files.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 5 passing
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run lint`
- generated the exact BOOSTXL-AUDIO archive and independently parsed 231 pads, 1,181 tracks, 111 vias, 72 components, 170 nets, six schematic sheets, and the closed board outline
- verified the generated BOOSTXL-AUDIO bounds are exactly 2300 × 3000 mil (58.42 × 76.20 mm) with clockwise winding, matching TI's original native Altium file
- Altium 365 Viewer loaded exporter output with SCH, PCB, 3D, and BOM views, and rendered the routed PCB successfully

title: Add symbols to capacitor and resistor imports
description: Retains original EasyEDA schematic graphics for imported capacitors and resistors without altering their electrical model or footprint behavior.
body:
## Summary

- preserve the original EasyEDA schematic drawing through the `symbol` prop when generating `<capacitor />` and `<resistor />` primitives
- omit nested EasyEDA symbol ports for passive primitives so their native electrical ports are not duplicated
- add regression coverage for capacitor paths, resistor rectangles, source/schematic port counts, and the real C62857 eight-pad capacitor array from #450

## Why

The dedicated capacitor and resistor import paths generated the correct primitive and footprint, but did not forward the symbol produced from the EasyEDA source. As a result, imported passive components lost their original schematic appearance.

Passive primitives already create their electrical ports. Reusing the chip symbol verbatim would create another set through nested `<port />` elements, so passive symbol generation keeps the EasyEDA drawing while relying on the primitive's native ports.

## Impact

Imported capacitors and resistors now retain their EasyEDA schematic graphics without changing their electrical model or footprint behavior. C62857 demonstrates that the full four-capacitor EasyEDA drawing is preserved for a multi-element passive package.

## Validation

## Summary

- Route net-derived parent connections to a child breakout point instead of the child's internal PCB pad.
- Reuse one breakout-aware PCB endpoint conversion for both direct-trace and net-derived Simple Route JSON connections.
- Extend the existing breakout regression and update its PCB and autorouting-phase snapshots.

## Root cause

Breakout substitution was only applied while building direct trace connections. Connections assembled from source nets always serialized each physical `pcb_port`, so a parent connection through a net could target the child's internal pad and bypass the breakout endpoint and its preserved child trace.

The parent routing scope now receives the `pcb_breakout_point` as its endpoint, while the child routing scope continues to route from the physical pad to that same point.

title: Fix default breakout routing with one-point nets
description: Fixes default breakout routing to omit net-derived autorouter connections with fewer than two physical points, allowing legitimate one-point connections to copper planes and treating empty multi-stage autorouting phases as no-ops.
body:
## What changed

- omit net-derived autorouter connections that still have fewer than two physical points after breakout-point processing
- preserve legitimate one-point connections that terminate into a configured copper plane
- treat empty multi-stage autorouting phases as no-ops instead of reporting a missing preceding-stage output
- convert the merged default-breakout repro into a passing zero-DRC test and update affected phase snapshots

## Root cause

A trace from a breakout pin to an abstract net produced both the valid pin-to-breakout connection and a second net connection containing only the same PCB port. The default breakout phase tolerated that malformed connection, but the following fanout phase rejected it because it had no target beyond the pad. Once the malformed connection was removed, Core also attempted the follow-up stage of the now-empty phase and reported a missing preceding-stage output.

## Impact

Default `<breakout>` routing can now finish without requiring a dummy second component or explicit autorouter props. Parent routing proceeds from the breakout point normally, while source-only plane drops remain supported.

## Validation

- `bun test tests/breakout --timeout 30000` — 17 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`

title: Orient enclosure apertures from the component frame
description: Prefer footprint-local cutoutApertureDirection over insertionDirection, preserving continuous aperture axis through component rotation and bottom-layer transforms, and deriving horizontal aperture profile roll from the PCB component frame.
body:
## Summary

- prefer footprint-local `cutoutApertureDirection` over `insertionDirection`, with nearest-edge detection remaining the fallback when neither is authored
- preserve the continuous aperture axis through component rotation and bottom-layer transforms instead of quantizing it to a wall direction
- anchor the transformed axis at the component datum so the enclosure solver can choose the first wall it intersects
- derive horizontal aperture profile roll from the PCB component frame rather than CAD asset alignment offsets

## Layering

All prerequisites for this final layer are merged:

- #3166 — `assembly.device` compatibility container
- #3174 — staged two-part solver integration
- #3180 — separate base and lid CAD components
- #3196 — component body, aperture offsets and explicit depth
- tscircuit/3d-viewer#974 — compatibility appearance controls for the assembled enclosure

This PR is now rebased onto Core `v0.0.1670` and contains only the component-relative aperture-axis layer.

## Circuit JSON compatibility

This deliberately preserves the existing synthetic enclosure representation. It does not emit unreleased typed enclosure records or persist viewer appearance state in Circuit JSON.

## Engineering guidance

This PR also adds the repository-local geometry rules learned while implementing the axis transform: explicit frame declarations, canonical direction names, composed transforms, proper bottom-layer rotations, and discriminating geometry tests. Keeping the guidance with the implementation prevents the same frame defects from returning.

## Testing

title: Reproduce default breakout one-point net error
description: Reproduces a bug where default breakout routing emits a one-point net connection, ensuring that no connection has fewer than two points during autorouting.
body:
## Summary

- reproduce default `<breakout>` routing emitting a one-point net connection
- use no explicit autorouter, fanout, or routing-constraint props
- preserve the enclosing subcircuit, outside R1, and parent VCC traces from the real hierarchical case
- capture both the PCB result and the autorouting phase inputs
- keep the expected behavior as a `test.failing` regression

This PR intentionally contains no production-code fix and no assertion for the separate parent-routing endpoint bug.

## Bug

A manual port-based `<breakoutpoint>` with no `autorouter` prop makes Core split breakout routing into a default escape phase and a fanout phase. For a trace from `U1.pin1` to `net.VCC`, Core emits these as separate connections:

```text
source_net_*: [U1.pin1]
breakout:...: [U1.pin1, breakoutPoint]
```

The fanout phase receives the one-point `source_net_0` connection and fails with:

```text
FanoutSolver: connection "source_net_*" has no target beyond its BGA pad
```

The test inspects every generated routing-phase input and requires that no connection have fewer than two points. It also requires that routing complete without a `pcb_autorouting_error` once the malformed connection is fixed.

Using `autorouter="auto"` avoids this default phase split and hides the failure. The outside R1 and its parent VCC connections intentionally remain in this repro, although they cannot route while the child breakout phase fails. Fixing this bug will let the same hierarchical circuit advance to the separate parent-route/breakout-endpoint issue without that prop or an extra component.

## Validation

- `BUN_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 bun test tests/breakout/default-breakout-one-point-net.test.tsx --timeout 30000`
- `bun test tests/breakout/default-breakout-one-point-net.test.tsx --timeout 30000`
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`

title: Add repro for incorrect component bounds on rotated rectangular pads
description: Adds a regression repro for jlcpcb:C1526234 placed at -90 next to a cap0402, demonstrating incorrect component bounds due to unrotated pad dimensions.
body:
Adds a regression repro for `jlcpcb:C1526234` placed at `-90°` next to a `cap0402`.

The generated `pcb_component` bounds incorrectly overlap C2 by approximately `0.64mm`, even though the actual courtyards have a clear gap of approximately `0.996mm`.

## Root cause demonstrated

The pad centers are transformed according to the component rotation, but the width and height of non-square rectangular pads are not rotated when calculating the component bounds.

## Snapshot annotations

- Red dashed: generated `pcb_component` bounds
- Red filled: false `0.64mm` overlap
- Magenta: actual courtyards
- Green: real `0.996mm` courtyard clearance

## Scope

This PR only adds the repro and snapshot. It does not implement the bounds calculation fix.

Core now uses the latest capacity autorouter behavior. The observable routing changes are captured in the affected SVG fixtures. The single-pin fixture no longer accepts a transient, unrouted snapshot.

## Root cause of the single-pin snapshot regression

The fixture placed the testpoint pad only 0.028 mm from the board edge, below the required 0.200 mm copper-to-edge clearance. Since placement checks became asynchronous and invalid placement began skipping autorouting, `circuit.render()` captured the circuit before those checks settled. Refreshing snapshots therefore accepted an unrouted PCB without asserting that a `pcb_trace` existed.

The fixture now uses valid explicit placement, awaits `renderUntilSettled()`, and checks placement errors, autorouting errors, and PCB trace count.

title: Fix copper pour bounds for offset boards
description: Fixes copper pour rendering to correctly follow the center of rectangular boards that are offset from the origin, ensuring accurate automatic copper pours and preserving explicit outlines.
body:
## Summary

- derive the default copper-pour outline from the rendered `pcb_board` center, width, and height
- preserve explicit copper-pour outlines and custom board outlines
- add a visual regression test for a board centered away from the PCB origin

## Root cause

When a rectangular board used `boardAnchorPosition`, the rendered `pcb_board.center` moved away from `(0, 0)`. Copper-pour rendering left `outline` undefined, so the solver synthesized bounds as `-width / 2 ... width / 2` and `-height / 2 ... height / 2`, ignoring the board center. The pour therefore stayed centered on the origin instead of following the board.

## Impact

Automatic copper pours now follow rectangular boards whose center is offset, including boards positioned with `boardAnchorPosition`. Existing explicit pour and polygon board outlines remain authoritative.

title: Check copper pours against board edges
description: Extends the copper edge clearance check to include copper pours, ensuring they do not violate board edge clearances and reporting violations through the existing placement-check pipeline.
body:
## What changed

- extend `checkCopperToBoardEdgeClearance` to include `pcb_copper_pour` elements
- support rectangular, polygon, and BRep pours, including BRep bulge arcs
- report violations through the existing placement-check pipeline
- document the additional copper geometry covered by the check

## Why

Copper-pour outlines can extend beyond a resized board without producing a placement error. The existing board-edge check covered vias, SMT pads, and plated holes, but omitted copper pours entirely.

## Impact

Designs now receive a `pcb_placement_error` when a copper pour is outside the board outline or violates `min_board_edge_clearance`. Pours at or above the configured clearance continue to pass.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 174 passing
- `bun run build`
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `git diff --check`

title: Warn on excessive schematic component vertical padding
description: Add a schematic check for excessive empty space above or below side-mounted pins, emitting warnings for excessive top or bottom padding.
body:
## Summary

- add a schematic check for excessive empty space above or below side-mounted pins
- emit `schematic_component_styling_warning` with `styling_issue_type: "excessive_top_padding"` or `"excessive_bottom_padding"`
- add `runAllSchematicChecks` and include it in `runAllChecks`
- ignore custom symbols, top/bottom-only pins, and components with fewer than two side pins
- add a rendered schematic SVG snapshot covering excessive padding on both vertical edges

## Why

Overly tall box-style schematic components can leave large blank areas around their pins, making otherwise small connectors and chips consume unnecessary space. This catches that common layout mistake on both vertical edges while keeping the threshold relative to the component's pin spacing.

## Dependency

Uses `schematic_component_styling_warning` from `circuit-json@0.0.467`, introduced by tscircuit/circuit-json#700.

## Validation

- `bun test` (168 tests, including top-only, bottom-only, and SVG snapshot coverage)

- Biome formatting and `git diff --check`

title: fix: enforce shape-accurate copper clearance against polygon board edges
description: Add a unified copper-to-board-edge placement check for vias, SMT pads, and plated holes, ensuring accurate clearance measurements against polygon board edges and reporting violations.
body:
## Summary

- add a unified copper-to-board-edge placement check for vias, SMT pads, and plated holes
- measure circle, rectangle, rounded rectangle, rotated rectangle, oval/pill, rotated pill, and polygon copper against `pcb_board.outline` (with rectangular fallback)
- model rounded copper exactly, including `rect_border_radius` / `corner_radius` on SMT and plated-hole rectangular pads
- honor `min_board_edge_clearance`, preserve the legacy `checkViasOffBoard` API, and register the unified check in `runAllPlacementChecks`
- report the offending circuit element ID together with measured and required clearances
- use branded component IDs and `transformation-matrix` for component and pad rotations
- add regression fixtures for chamfered-corner vias, rotated plated pills on angled edges, rounded corners near chamfers, below-minimum clearance, and equivalent passing geometry
- add one SVG snapshot showing a via, plated hole, and SMT pad outside the board, with placement-error assertions

## Root cause

Via placement used only the board's rectangular width/height bounds, while SMT-pad and plated-hole copper had no direct board-edge placement check. That missed polygon cut corners and shape/rotation-specific copper extents. Sharp-corner approximations also produce false positives for rounded rectangular copper near angled edges.

## Visual snapshot

![Via, plated hole, and SMT pad outside the board](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tscircuit/checks/9f4bcb8096919d2438b8a1d9ec26d4a8d9ea8545/tests/lib/__snapshots__/copper-outside-board.snap.svg)

The fixture verifies that the via, plated hole, and SMT pad each produce a `pcb_placement_error`.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 161 tests passed, 6 snapshots, 406 assertions
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`

title: Restart poisoned footprinter WASM workers
description: Implements a supervised batch processing system for footprinter population that restarts the WASM workers upon encountering errors, preventing infinite retry loops and ensuring efficient resource usage.
body:
## Summary

- run footprinter population in supervised 1,000-component child batches so Manifold WASM is periodically recycled
- detect the observed Emscripten `Aborted(). Build with -sASSERTIONS...` failure, flush completed rows, and restart in a fresh process
- stop after three rapid WASM aborts instead of creating an infinite retry loop
- keep the workflow's 240-minute global deadline and existing null-retry behavior

## Root cause

The four-hour production run processed components normally for about 76 minutes, then the long-lived Manifold WASM module entered an aborted state. Every later conversion failed even though affected components, including C696190, converted successfully in a fresh process. Network requests and permanent-null writes continued, so the poisoned process wasted the remainder of the run.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 223 passed
- `bun test tests/footprinter-population-restarts.test.ts` — 5 passed
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bun run format:check`
- `git diff --cached --check`

The affected production run was canceled; rows already committed to D1 and objects already cached in R2 were preserved.

title: Add shared EasyEDA R2 component cache
description: Add a fetch-through R2 cache for raw EasyEDA component JSON, keyed by normalized LCSC number, to reduce duplicate upstream traffic and improve efficiency in component fetching.
body:
## Summary

- add a fetch-through R2 cache for raw EasyEDA component JSON, keyed by normalized LCSC number
- expose `GET /api/easyeda_components/:lcsc` with the `easyeda_component_details` top-level response convention
- support R2-only probes with `?cache_only=true` and `R2-HIT`, `R2-MISS`, and `R2-STALE` response metadata
- cache successful payloads for 90 days and definitive not-found responses for 6 hours
- route footprinter population through the shared cache and report positive hits, negative hits, and fills
- limit cache fills to 2 components/second (approximately the existing 4 EasyEDA requests/second) and preserve the 403 cooldown

## Why

Raw EasyEDA footprint payloads were fetched independently by each caller and discarded after conversion. Persisting them in a shared cache prevents duplicate upstream traffic, lets other tscircuit services reuse the same payload, and makes future footprinter re-indexing possible without refetching every component.

## Infrastructure

Provisioned these R2 buckets in the existing Cloudflare account:

- `tscircuit-easyeda-component-cache` (production)
- `tscircuit-easyeda-component-cache-staging` (staging/preview)

The staging Worker was deployed from this branch and verified with a real C2906861 miss-to-hit cycle. The stored payload was then read directly from the staging R2 object, and the population cache client parsed the R2 hit through `EasyEdaJsonSchema` without invoking a fill.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 218 passing
- `bun run test --cwd cf-proxy` — 150 passing
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bunx tsc --noEmit --project cf-proxy/tsconfig.json`
- `bun run format:check`
- `git diff --check`
- staging Worker deployment and live R2 hit verification

## Deployment

After merge, deploy the production Worker before starting another population run so `/api/easyeda_components/:lcsc` is available on `jlcsearch.tscircuit.com`.

## Summary

- merge partial runtime platform overrides with eval's built-in platform defaults
- preserve custom autorouter, SPICE, footprint-library, footprint-parser, and static-file-loader entries
- add a regression test for the cache-only platform config supplied by `tsci dev`

RunFrame for the CLI supplies a partial `platformConfig` containing its local cache engine. `createExecutionContext` treated any supplied platform object as a complete platform configuration, so eval skipped `getPlatformConfig()` and dropped `footprintLibraryMap.kicad`. Consequently, `kicad:*` footprints worked in the web editor but failed in `tsci dev` with “No footprint resolver is configured for library \"kicad\".”

## Impact

CLI users retain CLI-specific platform overrides while receiving the same built-in KiCad and JLCPCB footprint resolvers as web users.

## Summary

- add a responsive gallery for projects with multiple static circuit files
- keep the searchable file selector and add a compact gallery action beside it
- load pre-rendered dist assets with a 3D-first fallback chain
- support opening the gallery from either the file browser or a `gallery` URL flag
- preserve file/tab URL state when moving between the gallery and circuit previews
- add a Cosmos fixture backed by checked-in CLI-generated 3D, PCB, schematic, and circuit JSON assets
- document the static asset convention

## Why

`tsci build --site` can expose every board in a project, but the static viewer previously required users to choose files from a text-only selector. This makes multi-board sites visual and easier to explore without fetching every circuit JSON up front.

Gallery cards derive sibling preview URLs from each `fileStaticAssetUrl`, preferring `3d.png` and falling back to PCB and schematic PNG/SVG outputs.

## Reviewer demo

Run `bun run cosmos` and open the **example57-static-build-gallery** fixture. It starts in the gallery with three real 3D thumbnails generated using `tsci build --site --all-images`. Select a card to open the interactive circuit preview, then use the gallery icon beside the regular file selector to return.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 44 tests passed
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`

title: Speed up Pipeline7 exact-geometry DRC by 8.7× on srj18 sample 1
description: Replaces board-size cutoffs with a DRC-validated adaptive repair flow, optimizing the exact-geometry DRC stage to achieve an 8.65 speedup on srj18 sample 1 while maintaining zero final DRC errors.
body:
## What changed

- replace board-size cutoffs with a DRC-validated adaptive repair flow
  - try the inexpensive safe-layer portfolio for structurally eligible two-layer routes
  - accept it only when the portfolio's real final DRC evaluation reports zero errors
  - otherwise discard the probe and run the full portfolio from the original routes
- index connection-to-net and connection-to-route lookups during repeated HD-route conversion
- derive the DRC spatial-index cell size from copper geometry and clearance
- disable redundant speculative broad-force attempts inside each targeted exact-DRC branch
  - Pipeline7's explicit top-level broad portfolio branch remains available
  - the dependency option defaults to enabled, preserving other callers
- cover fast-probe acceptance, multilayer bypass, dirty-probe fallback, and the explicit broad-fallback configuration

There are no connection-count, route-count, or board-size thresholds in the selection logic.

Supporting dependency PR: [tscircuit/high-density-repair03#70](https://github.com/tscircuit/high-density-repair03/pull/70).

## Why

On srj18 sample 1, `exactGeometryDrcForceImproveSolver` was dominated by a full preliminary branch portfolio, repeated linear route/connection scans, and a spatial index whose cells became too coarse on large layouts.

Aggregate profiling exposed a second bottleneck: each targeted branch repeated speculative broad repulsion after its targeted candidates stalled, even though `GlobalDrcBranchPortfolioSolver` already owns an explicit broad branch. On the captured sample 4 exact-DRC input, those nested broad candidates consumed roughly 102 seconds and none was accepted.

The new controls are based on algorithm structure and measured DRC outcomes rather than arbitrary board-size thresholds.

## Sample 1 target

Using synchronized current-main and PR checkouts with identical dependencies, the isolated exact-geometry DRC stage improved from a **3,594.42 ms median on main** to **415.40 ms on this branch**: **8.65× faster** (88.4% less time).

Both versions produced 205 routes with zero final DRC errors.

| this PR | 415.40 ms |
| speedup | **8.65×** |

A later full local srj18 sample 1 run completed in 11.42s with the optimized exact stage at 415.22ms, 184 vias, and zero relaxed DRC errors.

title: Eliminate false disconnected-pad DRC failures for preloaded traces
description: Fixes false disconnected-pad DRC failures for preloaded traces that touch pad edges, ensuring accurate DRC evaluations without altering the actual routing.
body: ## Scope This PR contains only the DRC evaluator fix. The dataset01 dependency update is isolated in [PR #2099](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2099), and the source dataset corrections remain in [dataset PR #127](https://github.com/tscircuit/autorouting-dataset-01/pull/127). ## Problem After dataset PR #127 regenerates the complete circuit018 board, a valid preloaded solder-jumper trace between `pcb_port_27` and `pcb_port_28` ends exactly on the rectangular pad edge. The copper is connected, but Circuit JSON DRC reports: > Trace `pcb_port_27 → pcb_port_28` is missing a connection to `pcb_port_27`. ## What this PR fixes For benchmark/debugger DRC conversion only, an original preloaded trace endpoint is attached to a pad when all of these are true: 1. The trace declares that pad in `connectsTo`. 2. The endpoint physically touches the rectangular pad within `1e-6`. 3. The endpoint is on the pad's layer. The DRC-only endpoint is then normalized to the pad center with its `pcb_port_id`. The real route is not changed, and internal repair scoring keeps the old behavior by default. A regression test proves a real 0.01 mm gap still fails. ## Visual proof — same board and same route - Before: main evaluator + corrected dataset circuit018 → 1 false missing-pad DRC. - After: this PR + the same circuit and route → 0 DRC errors. - Both runs used 16 vias; the copper geometry did not change. ## Why the GitHub same-machine comment shows 0 improved That bot run installed the currently published dataset, not dataset PR #127. Its old circuit018 fails for a different reason: two routed traces have only a **0.079 mm clearance gap**. Both main and this PR correctly report that same old-data failure, so **98.8% → 98.8% and 0 improved is expected**. PR #2099 supplies the corrected dataset revision separately. ## Validation - Focused corrected circuit018: 1 false DRC before → 0 after. - Full dataset01 with PR #2099: 85/85 complete, 100% relaxed DRC, 0 timeouts. - Positive pad-edge regression and negative 0.01 mm real-gap regression pass. - Relevant relaxed-DRC and Pipeline9 tests pass. - `bunx tsc --noEmit` - `bun run build` - No benchmark snapshots are committed.

body:
## What changed

- Add a guarded dual-candidate tiny-hypergraph portfolio for 30–99 route graphs.
- Evaluate the trace-density-aware candidate only when the legacy result predicts meaningful downstream failure pressure and concentrated port usage.
- Select the alternative when it materially disperses port concentration without PF regression, or when PF sum, squared PF, max PF, concentration, and segment count all improve together.
- Release the losing solver before detailed routing to avoid retaining both graph states.
- Record candidate and per-phase benchmark telemetry.
- Pin tiny-hypergraph commit `5e428bd5e88a5a74afed195c179783896aef4ca0` from tscircuit/tiny-hypergraph#165.
- Remove behavior-independent high-density A* overhead with numeric grid ids, explicit node construction, cached immutable via ancestry, an equivalent hole-sifting heap, optional visualization-history capture, and one shared future-penalty scan for each neighbor's `g`/`h` scores.
- Share planar point/edge obstacle queries through blocker-only per-layer indexes, flatten immutable future-connection points, cache future trace segments, and skip a redundant argument-less progress calculation.
- Spatially index route-stitch clearance geometry by copper layer and cache same-net lookups, while retaining the original exact clearance and endpoint-escape checks.
- Use tiny-hypergraph's compact typed candidate state instead of explicitly forcing sparse `Map` storage.
- Pin high-density-repair01 commit `8eaa775e7c7a2c32c12a82da4edef22477549027` from tscircuit/high-density-repair01#16, conservatively pruning remote segment pairs before force-projection exact geometry.

## Why

Minimizing legacy global-region cost in isolation was not a universal win: several configurations shortened high-density routing but shifted more work into exact-geometry DRC repair. The portfolio spends extra global-routing time only when completed-topology diagnostics predict lower total downstream work.

The first six-dataset same-machine run of the global-routing changes improved aggregate runtime by 1.55%, completion from 490/587 to 495/587, DRC passes from 266 to 268, and timeouts from 96 to 91. Every selected candidate won and the selected subset was 30.8% faster, showing that selector recall—not candidate quality—was the limiting factor. That was still too small as a universal performance win, so the final patch also removes detailed-routing hot-loop overhead without changing the search policy.

## Follow-up selector tuning

Both candidates were profiled for every evaluated SRJ19/SRJ20 case and every current timeout. End-to-end matched trials used fresh one-worker processes and equal 150 second caps.

The tuned selector adds five candidates across the observed benchmark population. The full audit preserves primary routing for all other rejected candidates, including known regressions.

| Dataset/sample | Primary | Alternative | Outcome |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| SRJ19 48 | 150 s timeout | 77.2 s complete | timeout converted |
| SRJ19 91 | 150 s timeout | 148.7 s complete | timeout converted in isolated run |
| SRJ19 117 | 150 s timeout | 95.4 s complete | timeout converted |
| SRJ20 132 | 65.9 s, 4 DRC errors | 58.1 s, DRC pass | 11.9% faster; 166 → 146 vias |
| SRJ20 189 | 43.2 s, 9 DRC errors | 35.0 s, DRC pass | 19.0% faster; 130 → 114 vias |

Negative controls rejected broader policies: SRJ20 sample 6 changed an 81.1 second completion into a timeout, sample 143 slowed 13.7%, SRJ19 sample 173 remained a high-density timeout, SRJ20 sample 119 remained an exact-repair timeout, and SRJ19 sample 121 was neutral.

## Detailed-routing speedup

A more aggressive trace-density factor was rejected after it lowered every tiny-stage pressure metric on promising SRJ19 cases but merely moved their timeout into high-density or exact-geometry repair. CPU profiling then identified behavior-independent overhead in the downstream A* loop.

Matched one-worker trials on eight high-density-heavy dataset01 cases retained identical high-density iteration counts, via counts, DRC messages, completion, and DRC status in every case:

| Metric | PR baseline | Optimized | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| High-density route time | 20.84 s | 13.29 s | -36.2% (1.57x faster) |
| End-to-end time | 43.24 s | 35.86 s | -17.1% (1.21x faster) |
| Completed / relaxed DRC | 8 / 8 | 8 / 8 | identical |

The larger SRJ18 sample 11 control retained 206,760 high-density iterations, 179 vias, and zero DRC errors. Its high-density phase fell from 27.48 to 18.23 seconds (-33.7%, 1.51x faster), and total time fell from 54.22 to 44.71 seconds (-17.5%). A same-process memory comparison on dataset01 sample 32 reduced maximum RSS from 858 MB to 842 MB and peak footprint from 662 MB to 625 MB.

The latest follow-up was measured against commit `4b97a6c` on the same eight cases. It retained byte-identical final output in every case while adding another 13.9% detailed-routing and 5.5% end-to-end reduction. A separate matched panel measured another 1.5% detailed-routing reduction from the progress guard. Applying those ratios to the preceding exact comparison puts the accepted stack at approximately **1.85x faster in detailed A*** and **22% faster end-to-end** than the original PR baseline.

| Follow-up metric | `4b97a6c` | Spatial query sharing | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| High-density route time | 17.18 s | 14.79 s | -13.9% |
| End-to-end time | 40.59 s | 38.34 s | -5.5% |

On SRJ18 sample 11, the follow-up alone reduced detailed routing from 21.65 s to 19.35 s (-10.6%) with the same 206,760 iterations, 179 vias, zero DRC errors, and byte-identical output. The cleaned final sample-32 memory run used 841 MB maximum RSS and a 623 MB peak footprint, slightly below `4b97a6c` at 842 MB / 625 MB.

The full experiment ledger is checked in at `experiments/tiny-hypergraph-balanced-routing.md`.

## Route-stitching speedup

The next profile found 710 tentative stitches scanning as many as 14,968
segments and 370 vias on dataset01 sample 32, producing 3.56 million same-net
checks. Dynamic R-tree indexes reduce that to 6,086 checks (-99.8%), while all
nearby candidates still run the original exact geometry tests.

Across the same eight dense dataset01 cases, this follow-up preserved iteration
counts, vias, DRC results, and byte-for-byte final output in every case:

| Metric | `125edc34` | Indexed stitching | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| End-to-end time | 41.22 s | 36.60 s | -11.2% |
| Stitch phase | 3.26 s | 0.147 s | -95.5% |

SRJ18 sample 11 was also byte-identical and improved end-to-end from 48.38 s
to 43.24 s (-10.6%), with stitch time falling from 3.35 s to 44 ms (-98.7%).
SRJ23 sample 39 was byte-identical and improved from 31.87 s to 31.56 s, with
stitch time falling from 300 ms to 9 ms. A matched memory pair increased peak
RSS from 833 MB to 864 MB and footprint from 639 MB to 667 MB (about 3-4%, still
below the 1 GB safety ceiling).

## Force-projection and compact-state speedups

The final profile found force projection evaluating exact segment-distance
geometry for every same-layer route pair. A live AABB lower bound now rejects
pairs separated by at least their required clearance; remaining pairs retain
the exact original order, distance calculation, and projection behavior.

Across the same eight dense dataset01 cases, force-improvement time fell from
3.536 s to 2.063 s (-41.7%, 1.71x faster) and end-to-end time fell 3.75%. Every
high-density iteration count, via count, DRC result, and output hash remained
identical. SRJ18 sample 11 was also byte-identical and reduced force time from
1.328 s to 0.703 s (-47.1%).

Enabling tiny-hypergraph's merged compact typed candidate storage reduced its
phase by 11.6% on a separate matched dense panel with identical final region
costs and output. It is bounded by legal incident hops, avoiding the memory
hazard of the former dense port-by-region allocation.

## Final official same-machine benchmark

The exact final head (`54191bc`) completed all six datasets and 587 scenarios.
Compared with current main on the same machine, aggregate scenario time fell
15.3%; P50/P60/P70/P80 fell 26.4%/25.8%/27.5%/30.3%; completion increased from
492 to 510; relaxed DRC passes increased from 266 to 271; and timeouts fell
from 94 to 76. There were 22 improved outcomes and zero regressions.

The result is broad: every dataset improved every non-timeout-capped reported
percentile. Dataset01 P95 improved 36.7% (1.58x), SRJ18 completion improved
12.5 percentage points, SRJ19 completion improved 5.5 points, and SRJ20 P50
improved 37.4% while DRC improved 2.0 points.

A paired-only region audit excludes main timeouts that never emitted tiny
metrics. Across 492-493 directly comparable cases, summed best max region cost
changed +0.24%, summed best total region cost +2.37%, final max occupancy
-0.13%, and squared occupancy -0.54%. This stays comfortably inside the ~20%
region-cost guardrail.

## Validation

- `bun test tests/solvers/tinyhypergraph-candidate-portfolio.test.ts`
- `bun test tests/single-high-density-route-solver.test.ts tests/data-structures/single-route-candidate-priority-queue.test.ts tests/features/never-fail-growth-high-density/pipeline7-integration.test.ts tests/features/high-density-future-cost-cmn3.test.ts`
- `bun test tests/features/pipeline7-full-pipeline-svg-frames.test.ts tests/pipeline-stage-debug-runner.test.ts tests/high-density-solver-failed-node-visualization.test.ts`
- `bun test tests/stitch-solver/collision-aware-stitch-selection-visual.test.ts tests/stitch-solver/multilayer-connection-stitch.test.ts tests/stitch-solver/single-high-density-route-stitch-gap-bridge.test.ts tests/bugs/bugreport44-0ec411-source-net-0-stitch.test.ts tests/bugs/bugreport46-ac4337-source-net-23-stitch-repro.test.ts tests/features/pipeline7-dataset01-circuit107-open-stitch-route.test.ts`
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`
- `git diff --check`
- high-density-repair01: `bun test` (14 pass), `bunx tsc --noEmit`, `bun run format:check`
- End-to-end matched Pipeline 7 trials for accepted candidates and negative controls
- Complete tiny-stage candidate audit across evaluated SRJ19/SRJ20 cases and current timeouts
- 1,000 randomized priority-queue operation streams matched the legacy implementation's identity order

`bugreport88` was intentionally excluded from local testing due its prior RAM behavior. All routing trials used one worker; no timeout was increased.

## Summary

Document the Circuit JSON Z-up to glTF Y-up conversion and the rules for adding or changing model transforms:

- rotations must be remapped across the up-axis boundary
- bottom-layer placement is a proper rotation, not a three-axis inversion
- model formats have distinct normalization conventions
- transform boundaries must state frames, units, and point-vs-direction semantics
- geometry tests need off-axis probes and multiple rotations

Documentation only; no converter behavior changes.

body:
## Summary

- add a checked-in AP214 STEP model for a 0.12 mm stainless-steel BiscuitBoard stencil blank
- add a TypeScript generator using `manifold-3d` and `manifold-to-step`
- preserve the standard 75 mm × 55 mm outline, 2 mm corner radius, and five Ø2.2 mm mounting holes
- add a package script, locked dependencies, and regeneration documentation

## Why

This provides a manufacturer-ready mechanical stencil blank aligned to the standard BiscuitBoard clad mounting-hole pattern, while keeping the artifact reproducible from the project geometry.

## Validation

- `bunx biome check README.md package.json scripts/export-stencil-step.ts`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun test tests/biscuit-board.test.tsx tests/biscuit-board-autorouter.test.ts`
- deterministic regeneration comparison with the checked-in STEP file
- generator assertions: 75 × 55 × 0.12 mm bounds, five-hole topology, and 492.307720 mm³ volume

## Known unrelated test result

A full `bun test` run also exercised the existing RP2040 routing test, which failed because the autorouter could not find a route for `source_net_4:20`. The stencil-specific and directly relevant tests pass.

title: Add congestion severity metadata and deterministic tie-breaking
description: Adds congestion severity metadata and deterministic tie-breaking to improve routing analysis by providing clearer prioritization of congested regions based on failure probability and additional metrics.
body:
## Motivation

After duplicate congestion regions are merged and nearby components are found, the routing-difficulty result still does not give users or placement agents enough information to prioritize equivalent-looking problems.

A region currently exposes its failure probability and nearby components, but not how many planned point-to-point connections and electrical nets compete there or how many component bodies intersect the congested area. Regions with the same rounded probability also have no meaningful deterministic tie-breaker. That makes placement iteration noisy: an agent can spend time on a less constrained region while a more obstructed region with the same reported probability remains unresolved.

This PR makes the analyzer return the most consequential regions first and explains the physical facts behind that ordering.

## Before

```xml
<CongestedRegion probabilityOfFailure="2.1%" ...>
  <NearbyComponent name="U2" ... />
</CongestedRegion>
```

Two regions with the same probability looked equivalent even when one had more competing connections or more component bodies occupying the congestion region.

## After

```xml
<CongestedRegion
  severity="high"
  probabilityOfFailure="2.1%"
  connectionCount="5"
  netCount="2"
  componentsIntersectingRegion="1"
  ...
>
  <NearbyComponent
    name="U2"
    edgeDistance="0mm"
    overlapDepth="0.8mm"
    ...
  />
</CongestedRegion>
```

`connectionCount` counts planned point-to-point routing connections in the region. `netCount` counts their distinct root electrical nets. Keeping both distinguishes congestion from many independent nets from fanout branches belonging to one multi-pin net.

`componentsIntersectingRegion` clearly counts component bodies that intersect the congestion rectangle; it does not mean components overlap each other. The existing per-component `overlapDepth` retains the detailed geometric information.

`probabilityOfFailure` remains the single numeric risk value. `severity` is only its readable critical/high/medium/low classification; there is no duplicate severity score.

## What changed

- add a severity label derived directly from the existing failure probability
- report unique planned connection count and root-net count for each merged region
- report how many component bodies intersect each congestion region
- retain overlap depth on each individual nearby component instead of adding a redundant region-level maximum
- rank regions deterministically by:
  1. failure probability
  2. components intersecting the region
  3. connection count
  4. net count
  5. stable region coordinates
- update the analyzer string output, documentation, and regression coverage

## Why the ranking belongs here

`circuit-json-routing-analysis` owns region construction and has access to the routing nodes, connectivity, geometry, and nearby-component data required to rank them correctly. It returns the already-ranked array and string. The CLI remains a presentation-only consumer and requires no changes.

## Generality and safety

The implementation uses only routing-model and PCB-geometry data. It contains no:

- board-specific component names
- fixed board coordinates
- hardcoded pins
- BLDC-specific rules
- opaque weighted composite score
- fabricated movement suggestions

This keeps the result applicable to any circuit-json PCB.

## What this improves

- placement agents see the most important bottlenecks first
- equal-probability regions receive meaningful, repeatable ordering
- humans and agents can distinguish multi-net competition from single-net fanout
- each ranking decision is explainable from concise returned metrics
- the component-intersection field has unambiguous semantics
- repeated analyzer runs produce stable output suitable for placement feedback loops
- downstream consumers do not need to reproduce congestion-ranking logic

## Validation

- `bun test` — 8 passed
- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`

title: Prune remote projection segment pairs
description: Rejects projection segment pairs whose live axis-aligned bounds are separated by at least their required clearance, preserving original pair order and segment-distance calculations for interacting pairs, while avoiding additional spatial index allocation or changes to forceprojection parameters.
body:
## Summary

- reject projection segment pairs whose live axis-aligned bounds are separated by at least their required clearance
- preserve the original pair order and exact segment-distance/projection calculation for every pair that can interact
- avoid allocating an additional spatial index or changing any force/projection parameters

## Performance

Matched one-worker Pipeline 7 runs used dataset01 samples 32, 37, 39, 49, 58, 67, 73, and 77. Every case retained the same high-density iteration count, via count, DRC result, and byte-for-byte output hash.

| Metric | Baseline | This change | Delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Force-improvement time | 3.536 s | 2.063 s | **-41.7% (1.71x faster)** |
| End-to-end time | 34.081 s | 32.804 s | **-3.75%** |

SRJ18 sample 11 was also byte-identical; force improvement fell from 1.328 s to 0.703 s (-47.1%) and total time from 45.05 s to 42.75 s. SRJ23 sample 39 was byte-identical and effectively a control because force improvement is only about 0.1 s of its 32 s runtime.

The rejection is conservative: if either projected AABB interval is separated by `requiredDistance`, Euclidean segment distance cannot be below `requiredDistance`, so the original projection could not move either segment.

## Validation

- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- `bun run format:check`
- `bun test` (14 pass)
- `git diff --check`
- matched eight-case dataset01 panel: all outputs byte-identical
- SRJ18 sample 11 and SRJ23 sample 39: outputs byte-identical

title: Allow disabling speculative broad DRC fallbacks
description: Adds an optional enableBroadFallback control to GlobalDrcForceImproveSolver to disable redundant speculative broad-force candidates, improving performance without altering existing behavior.
body:
## What changed

- add an optional `enableBroadFallback` control to `GlobalDrcForceImproveSolver`
- preserve existing behavior by defaulting the option to `true`
- gate only the speculative per-iteration broad-force candidate path
- preserve the option through `getConstructorParams()`
- cover default behavior, disabled behavior, evaluator work, and output equivalence

## Why

`GlobalDrcBranchPortfolioSolver` already owns an explicit top-level broad branch. When a caller runs that portfolio, each targeted child solver can also repeat speculative broad repulsion after targeted candidates fail. Those nested candidates are expensive and may never be accepted.

Callers that already provide a deliberate outer broad strategy can now disable only the redundant inner attempts. This is an explicit algorithm choice, not a route-count, connection-count, or board-size threshold.

## Impact

On the exact Pipeline7 srj18 sample 4 portfolio input used by [tscircuit-autorouter#2102](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2102):

| Mode | Time | Final DRC issues | Routes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| default broad fallback | 106.12s | 34 | 114 |
| broad fallback disabled | 4.51s | 34 | 114 |
| improvement | **23.5×** | unchanged | unchanged |

The broad candidates consumed roughly 102 seconds and none was accepted. Existing callers remain unchanged because the new option defaults to enabled.

## Validation

- `bun test` — 61 passed
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run formatcheck`
- `git diff --check`

title: Make endpoint-aligned fanouts the default
description: Removes the opt-in flag for endpoint-aligned fanouts, making them the default behavior for all users, thus improving routing for dense fanouts without requiring additional configuration.
body:
## Summary

- remove the `preferOriginalEndpointTracks` opt-in from the public solver API
- prefer original downstream endpoint tracks and their legal source layer automatically
- retain compact and interstitial track strategies as fallback candidates for dense fanouts
- refresh the SRJ19 and RP2350A visual baselines that now use endpoint-aligned routing

## Root cause

PR #44 added endpoint-aware routing behind `preferOriginalEndpointTracks` and enabled it only for the SRJ29 benchmark adapter. The deployed Vercel datasets construct the same solver without that benchmark-only option, so they continued to use the older compact/source-track preference and produced visibly worse fanouts.

The solver now detects when a bus's real downstream endpoints occupy different perpendicular tracks and applies the endpoint-aware layer heuristic automatically. Synthetic straight-out targets keep the established layer-distribution behavior, while dense cases can still fall back to the prior compact/interstitial track candidates.

## Impact

All callers now get endpoint-aligned fanouts without knowing about a solver flag. The SRJ29 samples from #44 remain unchanged, while SRJ19 and deployed mixed-footprint/boundary samples use the improved default.

## Validation

- `bun test`: 68 pass, 0 fail
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run format:check`
- `git diff --check`
- `bun run build:site`

title: Prune redundant same-net copper cycles
description: Adds a topology-cleanup stage that removes redundant copper branches from the same electrical net while preserving routed trace attachments and clearance requirements.
body: ## What this adds This PR adds `PruneRedundantSameNetCopperSolver`, a topology-cleanup stage that runs after trace beautification and before nominal-width expansion. Beautified traces from the same electrical net can cross, join, or partially overlap and form a copper cycle. The cycle is electrically valid, but one branch is redundant—for example, a component-to-via branch when that component already reaches the via through other same-net copper. The new stage removes that redundant branch while preserving every routed trace attachment, fixed-via transition, and clearance requirement. Before: After: ## Pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Beautified traces] --> B[Group traces by electrical net] B --> C[Build an existing-copper graph] C --> D[Split at crossings, T-junctions, overlap endpoints, and trace attachments] D --> E[Add prefabricated-via transitions as fixed graph edges] E --> F{Does the net contain a cycle?} F -- No --> G[Keep the net unchanged] F -- Yes --> H[Select a deterministic minimum-cost tree from existing copper] H --> I[Trim leaves that are not real trace attachments] I --> J[Rebuild only traces that used a removed edge] J --> K{Clearance valid and all vias prefabricated?} K -- Yes --> L[Accept the pruned topology] K -- No --> M[Restore the original net] G --> N[Expand traces to nominal width] L --> N M --> N ``` In the router's full pipeline, this is one additional stage: ```text ... -> beautify-traces -> prune-redundant-same-net-copper (new) -> expand-traces -> ... ``` ## How it works 1. **Planarize existing copper** - Split same-layer segments at crossings, T-junctions, and overlap endpoints. - Split segments where an emitted trace attaches to the interior of another segment. - Represent required prefabricated-via transitions as fixed graph edges. 2. **Detect redundant topology** - Process each electrical net independently. - Skip nets whose copper graph is already acyclic. 3. **Choose the copper to retain** - Use deterministic, cost-ordered tree selection over edges that already exist. - Retain connectivity between every emitted trace endpoint. - Remove non-terminal leaves so no fragments of a deleted cycle remain. 4. **Rebuild the minimum necessary geometry** - Leave unaffected traces byte-for-byte unchanged. - Rebuild only demands whose original path crossed a pruned edge. - Route those demands over the retained existing-copper tree; the stage does not invent a new copper segment or layer transition. 5. **Validate or roll back** - Run the normal copper-clearance validation on the candidate result. - Reassert that every layer transition uses a prefabricated via. - If sharing the retained path at a demand's width would be unsafe, restore the entire original net instead of applying a partial cleanup. ## Why this is safe - Connectivity is defined by actual emitted trace attachments, including attachments inside another segment—not only abstract routing terminals. - Cleanup is isolated per net, so one unsafe net does not prevent safe nets from being pruned. - No new copper geometry or via is introduced; the output is composed from copper already emitted by the router. - Mixed-width nets are checked after reconstruction, and unsafe candidates are rolled back. - The existing trace metadata and endpoint-to-endpoint Circuit JSON contract are preserved. ## Observability The solution reports: - `sameNetCyclePruneCount`: cyclic nets successfully cleaned - `sameNetCyclePruneSkipCount`: cyclic nets restored after validation failed - `prunedSameNetEdgeCount`: redundant graph edges removed The pipeline visualization also exposes the cleaned same-net topology before trace expansion. ## Verification - `bun run test` — 32 passed, 0 failed - `bun run build` - `bun run format:check` - STM-display reproduction: removes the redundant C_MCU-to-via GND branch - RP2040 full-board regression: preserves routing and validates the cleanup stage in the pipeline - GitHub CI: test, type-check, format-check, and Vercel checks pass

- add a checked-in PCB/schematic snapshot fixture
- add a `tsci snapshot --ci` workflow that detects stale or missing committed snapshots and uploads diff artifacts

## Why

Future board PRs should expose deterministic PCB and schematic SVG changes directly in the diff, with CI enforcing that the snapshots match the TSX.

## Validation

- `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run build`
- `bun run snapshot:update`
- `bun run snapshot`
- `git diff --check -- . ':(exclude)**/*.snap.svg'`

The generated `.snap.svg` files contain whitespace emitted by the current tscircuit renderer, so the whitespace-only check excludes generated snapshots.
